subject: VAPA
overview: Plan about 30 minutes a day. The year moves through visual art fundamentals, ancient-world art (linked to sixth-grade history), perspective and design, music literacy and composition, world music, theatre, photography, stop-motion animation, dance, and a culminating portfolio and showcase. You don't need arts training: show the example image, recording or video, try the technique with your child, and coach with the specific cues and criteria in each lesson. Keep a sketchbook and a portfolio (physical and digital) all year, use clear criteria for critique, and record performances so your child can self-evaluate and see growth.

weeks.prep: Gather a sketchbook, HB, 2B and 4B pencils (B = softer, darker), an eraser and a fine marker. Set a timer for 30-second gestures and ask a family member to pose.
misconceptions: Thinking a 'good' blind contour looks realistic. It's an observation exercise; distorted results are normal and useful.
Spending too long on gesture drawings. Gesture captures movement and the line of action in seconds, not detail.

days.guide: Your child designs a cover with their name in a decorative lettering style, then starts an 'ideas I want to explore' page (subjects, media, questions) to return to all year.

questions.q: Why keep an 'ideas I want to explore' page?
questions.a: It records interests and inspiration to use for future projects, especially the final personal artwork.

days.guide: Your child fills a page with 20 line types and labels each with a mood word (e.g., jagged = tense, flowing curve = calm).

questions.q: How can a line show mood?
questions.a: Its direction, thickness, speed and shape suggest feelings: horizontal = calm, diagonal/zigzag = energy or tension, curvy = gentle.

days.guide: Three blind contours (never look at the paper) and three modified contours (glance occasionally) of the hand.

questions.q: What skill does blind contour build?
questions.a: Careful observation and eye–hand coordination.

days.guide: Ten 30-second gestures; start each with the line of action (a curve through the spine). Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.a: A single flowing line that shows the main direction and movement of a pose.

days.guide: Your child picks the best line drawing and writes two sentences about successful line choices.

questions.a: How thick or dark a line is; varying it adds emphasis and depth.

weeks.assessment_key: Sketchbook check: cover, ideas page, 20 labeled lines, 3 blind + 3 modified contours, 10 gestures. Reflection rubric: 4 = two sentences using specific art vocabulary (contour, line weight, gesture) tied to the drawing; 3 = one term; 2 = general; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Pencils, a blending stump or tissue, an egg (or white ball) and a desk lamp. Darken the room for Thursday.
misconceptions: Outlining shaded forms with a dark line. Show edges with changes in value instead.
Forgetting reflected light. The shadow side of a round object is slightly lighter near the bottom edge because light bounces up from the table.

days.guide: Draw a 9-step value scale using pressure and layering, white to black. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.a: How light or dark a tone or color is.

days.guide: Practice hatching, cross-hatching, stippling and blending in four boxes, each going light to dark.

questions.q: How do you make stippling darker?
questions.a: Place dots closer together.

days.guide: Turn a circle, square and triangle into a sphere, cube and cone by adding light and shadow from one direction.

questions.q: What's the difference between shape and form?
questions.a: Shape is flat (2D: length and width); form is 3D (length, width and depth).

days.guide: Light an egg with a lamp; draw it showing highlight, core shadow, reflected light and cast shadow.

questions.q: Where does the cast shadow fall?
questions.a: On the surface, on the side opposite the light source.

days.guide: Critique the egg with a checklist; redraw one area. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.a: Light that bounces off a nearby surface onto the shadow side of an object, making it slightly lighter.

weeks.assessment_key: Value scale: 9 even steps. Still life checklist: consistent light source, highlight, core shadow, reflected light, cast shadow, smooth gradations. 4 = all; 3 = one missing; 2 = two or three missing; 1 = flat.

weeks.prep: Tempera or watercolor (red, yellow, blue, white, black), brushes, a paper-plate palette and paper. Use one water cup for rinsing and change it only when muddy (water conservation).
misconceptions: Thinking hue and value are the same. Hue is the color name; value is how light or dark it is.
Thinking warm and cool colors are only about temperature. They also suggest mood and distance (warm advances, cool recedes).

days.guide: Paint a 12-part wheel mixing only primaries. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: What are the three tertiary colors next to orange?
questions.a: Red-orange and yellow-orange are the tertiaries on either side of orange.

days.guide: Paint a 7-step tint and shade strip; practice brush cleaning and saving water. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: How do you make a shade?
questions.a: Add black (a little at a time) to a hue.

days.guide: Paint the same simple landscape in warm analogous colors and in cool colors. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.a: Colors next to each other on the color wheel (e.g., red, red-orange, orange).

days.guide: Make a small abstract using a complementary pair to create a focal point. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Why do complementary colors make a strong focal point?
questions.a: Opposites create the highest contrast, so the eye goes there.

days.guide: Compare the two landscapes; write how color changed mood. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: What mood might cool colors create?
questions.a: Calm, peaceful, sad, cold or quiet.

weeks.assessment_key: Color wheel: 12 colors accurately mixed and ordered. Mood landscapes: same composition in warm analogous and cool palettes; written comparison names specific colors and resulting moods. Proficient = both complete with accurate explanation.

weeks.prep: Gather crayons, paper, textured household objects (screens, leaves, baskets, coins), magazines, scissors and glue. Choose a chair for the negative-space drawing.
misconceptions: Thinking texture must be real. Implied (visual) texture is drawn to look like a texture.
Thinking negative space is empty and unimportant. It shapes the subject and balances the composition.

days.guide: Make 10 crayon rubbings; draw implied versions of three. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What is the difference between actual and implied texture?
questions.a: Actual texture can be felt; implied texture only looks like it would feel a certain way.

days.guide: Draw only the spaces around and between the chair's legs and rungs. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.a: The empty space around and between objects.

days.guide: Find and label magazine images showing balance, emphasis, rhythm, contrast and unity. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What does emphasis mean in design?
questions.a: Making one part stand out as the focal point.

days.guide: Create a collage using at least three principles deliberately. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: How can you create rhythm in a collage?
questions.a: Repeat shapes, colors or lines in a regular or flowing pattern.

days.guide: Write a criteria checklist for a good composition; evaluate the collage. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Give one criterion for a strong composition.
questions.a: A clear focal point, balance, unity, varied but related elements.

weeks.assessment_key: Collage rubric: 4 = at least three principles clearly used and labeled, strong craftsmanship, self-made criteria applied with evidence; 3 = two principles; 2 = one; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Find images of the Lascaux cave paintings (France, about 17,000 years old), the Ishtar Gate (Babylon, c. 575 BCE, Pergamon Museum) and Assyrian lion-hunt reliefs (Nineveh, British Museum). Gather a brown paper bag, charcoal, earth-tone chalk pastels, and air-dry clay.
misconceptions: Thinking prehistoric art was just decoration. It may have had ritual, hunting or storytelling purposes.
Thinking cylinder seals were jewelry only. They were rolled on clay to sign or seal documents and goods.

days.guide: Study Lascaux; discuss what the animals may have meant. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.a: Horses, bulls/aurochs, deer, bison and others.

days.guide: Crumple a paper bag; draw animals with charcoal and earth-tone pastels. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What did prehistoric artists use for paint?
questions.a: Natural pigments like ochre (earth), charcoal and minerals mixed with water or fat.

days.guide: Study the Ishtar Gate and Assyrian reliefs; identify how they show power. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: How do the Assyrian lion reliefs show the king's power?
questions.a: The king is shown defeating powerful lions, proving his strength and right to rule.

days.guide: Carve a design into a clay cylinder; roll it onto flat clay. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What was a cylinder seal used for?
questions.a: To sign or mark ownership by rolling an impression into wet clay.

days.guide: Write how the cave art and seal connect to ancient art's purposes. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Name two purposes of ancient art.
questions.a: Ritual/religion, recording events, showing power, marking ownership, storytelling.

weeks.assessment_key: Cave art: animals drawn with natural colors on textured paper. Seal: carved design leaves a clear rolled impression. Reflection rubric: 4 = connects both works to specific purposes (ritual, power, ownership) with examples; 3 = one; 2 = vague; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Find an Egyptian tomb painting (e.g., Tomb of Nebamun, British Museum). Gather kraft paper or a paper bag, colored pencils, a gold marker, and grid paper.
misconceptions: Thinking Egyptian artists couldn't draw realistically. They followed conventions on purpose to show the most important view of each body part.
Thinking size shows distance in Egyptian art. Larger figures are more important (hierarchical scale).

days.guide: Analyze a tomb painting for composite view, hierarchical scale and registers. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.a: Showing each body part from its most recognizable angle: head and legs in profile, eye and shoulders from the front.

days.guide: Draw a figure on a grid using Egyptian proportions (about 18 squares from feet to hairline).

questions.q: Why did Egyptian artists use grids?
questions.a: To keep figure proportions consistent and follow traditional rules.

days.guide: Plan a 'tomb painting' of daily life in registers. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.a: Horizontal bands that organize scenes, like comic strip rows.

days.guide: Complete with Egyptian colors and a name cartouche. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.a: An oval enclosing a royal name in hieroglyphs.

days.guide: Explain conventions used and why they mattered. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Why did conventions matter to Egyptian beliefs?
questions.a: Tomb art was meant to last forever and help the dead in the afterlife, so figures had to be complete and clear.

weeks.assessment_key: Egyptian painting rubric: 4 = composite view, hierarchical scale, registers, cartouche and Egyptian colors, with explanation tied to beliefs; 3 = one missing; 2 = two missing; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Find black-figure and red-figure vases on the Metropolitan Museum website (e.g., works attributed to Exekias for black-figure; a red-figure krater). Gather orange and black paper, a white pencil, scissors, glue, and optional air-dry clay.
misconceptions: Mixing up black-figure and red-figure. Black-figure = black figures on orange clay; red-figure = orange figures on a black background.
Thinking vases were only decorative. They had everyday uses: storing, mixing and drinking.

days.guide: Learn amphora (two-handled storage jar), krater (wide bowl for mixing wine and water), kylix (shallow drinking cup); sketch each.

questions.q: What was a krater used for?
questions.a: Mixing wine with water.

days.guide: Compare black-figure and red-figure vases; list differences. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Why did red-figure allow more detail?
questions.a: Artists painted details with a brush on the orange figures instead of scratching them into black slip.

days.guide: Design a vase showing a myth or modern event with a Greek key border. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.a: A continuous border pattern of interlocking right-angle lines.

days.guide: Create the vase in black-figure style with cut paper or on clay. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: In black-figure, how were details added?
questions.a: Scratched (incised) through the black to show the orange clay.

days.guide: Present the story and evaluate the border. Treat it like a real event: quiet audience, a short spoken introduction and a bow; then debrief together using the week's rubric, starting with what went well.

questions.a: A horizontal band of decoration or figures.

weeks.assessment_key: Greek vase rubric: 4 = correct vase shape, clear narrative scene in black-figure style, neat Greek key border, explanation of story; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = style or border missing; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather a compass, protractor, colored markers, black ink or watercolor, a round brush, and long paper for a scroll. Find images of a Gandharan Buddha (Pakistan/Afghanistan region) and a Chinese Buddha (e.g., Longmen Grottoes) and a Chinese ink landscape (e.g., Fan Kuan's 'Travelers among Mountains and Streams').
misconceptions: Thinking radial symmetry is the same as mirror symmetry. Radial symmetry repeats around a center point like spokes.
Filling all space in Chinese landscapes. Empty space suggests mist, distance and calm.

days.guide: Draw concentric circles with a compass and divide them with a protractor (e.g., every 30°); create a radially symmetric mandala.

questions.a: Design elements repeat evenly around a center point.

days.guide: Compare Gandharan and Chinese Buddhas. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: How do Gandharan Buddhas show Greek and Roman influence?
questions.a: Wavy hair, realistic faces and toga-like robes with deep folds, like Greco-Roman sculpture.

days.guide: Practice Chinese brush strokes; paint bamboo stalks and leaves. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: How should you hold the brush for Chinese painting?
questions.a: Upright, moving from the arm, pressing and lifting to vary stroke width.

days.guide: Paint a vertical scroll landscape with ink washes: dark near, pale far, empty space for mist.

questions.q: How do you show distance with ink wash?
questions.a: Paint far mountains with pale, watery ink and less detail; near ones darker.

days.guide: Compare mandala and scroll and how each reflects cultural values. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What does a mandala often represent?
questions.a: The universe or a spiritual journey toward the center in Hindu and Buddhist traditions.

weeks.assessment_key: Mandala: accurate radial symmetry with compass/protractor. Ink landscape: at least three values, mist/empty space, vertical format. Comparison: connects each to culture's values (spiritual wholeness; harmony with nature). Proficient = all.

weeks.prep: Find Pompeii mosaics such as 'Cave Canem' (House of the Tragic Poet). Gather colored paper squares (about 1 cm) or dried beans, glue, cardboard, and grid paper. Find a short museum conservation video (e.g., Getty or the Met).
misconceptions: Gluing tesserae touching each other. Leave small even gaps (grout lines).
Thinking conservation means repainting old art. Conservators stabilize and protect art and try not to change the original.

days.guide: Study Pompeii mosaics; identify how tesserae create shading. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.a: One small tile piece in a mosaic.

days.guide: Sketch a mosaic design and plan colors on a grid. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Why plan colors on a grid first?
questions.a: To see how pieces will fit and show shading before gluing.

days.guide: Glue tesserae onto cardboard with even grout lines. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.a: By placing lighter and darker tiles in rows that follow the shape.

days.guide: Watch a conservation video; compare how 2D, 3D and digital works are preserved. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.a: Backing up files in multiple places and updating them to new formats.

days.guide: Display ancient-art pieces; critique your strongest using criteria. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.a: Chooses, organizes and cares for artworks in a collection or exhibition.

weeks.assessment_key: Mosaic: clear design, even grout lines, shading with tesserae. Critique rubric: 4 = uses own criteria with evidence about strongest work; 3 = criteria with little evidence; 2 = opinion only; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Ruler, pencil, photos of hallways and roads (printed). Orthogonals = lines that go back to the vanishing point.
misconceptions: Placing the vanishing point off the horizon. In one-point perspective it's always on the horizon line.
Slanting vertical lines. Verticals stay vertical; horizontals parallel to the picture stay horizontal.

days.guide: Trace orthogonals on photos to find vanishing points. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.a: At the vanishing point on the horizon line.

days.guide: Draw 8 boxes above, below and on the horizon. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: For a box above the horizon line, which side do you see?
questions.a: The bottom.

days.guide: Draw a hallway with doors and windows. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Why do doors farther down the hall look smaller?
questions.a: Objects appear smaller as they get farther away.

days.guide: Draw your bedroom with furniture in one-point perspective. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Where should the horizon line be?
questions.a: At your eye level as you look into the room.

days.guide: Self-check orthogonals with a ruler; fix errors. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.a: Objects appear shorter when they extend toward or away from the viewer.

weeks.assessment_key: Room drawing: 4 = horizon and vanishing point marked, all orthogonals converge, verticals vertical, furniture in perspective; 3 = 1–2 errors; 2 = several; 1 = none.

weeks.prep: Ruler, long paper (tape two sheets), colored pencils.
misconceptions: Placing vanishing points too close together. Spread them far apart (at the paper edges) to avoid distorted boxes.
Forgetting the leading edge. Start each box with a vertical line (the nearest corner).

days.guide: Draw boxes using two vanishing points. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.a: The vertical edge closest to the viewer, from which lines go to both vanishing points.

days.guide: Turn boxes into buildings with doors, windows and roofs. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.a: To the same vanishing point as the wall they're on.

days.guide: Draw a street-corner cityscape. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: How is two-point different from one-point perspective?
questions.a: Two-point uses two vanishing points and shows objects from a corner; one-point shows them straight on.

days.guide: Color using atmospheric perspective. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.a: Distant objects look lighter, cooler and less detailed.

days.guide: Revise one area after a parent's critique. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.a: Others spot errors and suggest improvements.

weeks.assessment_key: Cityscape: 4 = two vanishing points on the horizon, accurate converging lines, at least three buildings with details, atmospheric color; 3 = minor errors; 2 = inconsistent; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Graph paper, cardboard, tape, scissors. Prepare interview questions for a family member (what activities, how many people, comfort, light, accessibility needs).
misconceptions: Designing for yourself only. Good design starts with the user's needs.
Forgetting accessibility. Spaces should work for people with different abilities.

days.guide: Interview a family member about a reading nook or community space. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.a: So the design solves their real needs.

days.guide: Draw a floor plan to scale with accessibility features. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.a: Ramps, wide doorways (at least 32 inches), lever handles, reachable shelves, good lighting.

days.guide: Draw a perspective view of the design. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What does a scale like 1 square = 1 foot mean?
questions.a: Each square on the plan represents one foot in real life.

days.guide: Build a small cardboard model. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.a: To see the space in 3D and test the design.

days.guide: Present the design; explain how it meets needs. Set up a simple 'stage' and audience, have your child introduce the work, and hold applause until the end; afterward ask them to name one strength and one thing to improve before you add one specific comment.

questions.a: A flat side or front view of a building or wall.

weeks.assessment_key: Design presentation: 4 = floor plan to scale, perspective view, model, clear link to user needs including accessibility; 3 = one element weak; 2 = several missing; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Find WPA National Park posters (Library of Congress) and two modern public service posters. Gather poster paper, markers, a ruler.
misconceptions: Using too many colors and fonts. A limited palette and one or two lettering styles make a clearer message.
Writing too much text. Posters should be read in seconds.

days.guide: Analyze three posters for focal point, color and text. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: What makes WPA posters easy to read from a distance?
questions.a: Bold simple shapes, a limited color palette and large, clear lettering.

days.guide: Choose a message; sketch three thumbnail layouts. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.a: To try different layouts quickly before choosing the best one.

days.guide: Practice block and decorative lettering for the headline. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.a: The style and arrangement of letters.

days.guide: Create the final poster with a clear focal point and limited palette. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: How can you create a focal point?
questions.a: Make it largest, highest contrast, or place it where lines lead the eye.

days.guide: Ask two viewers what the message is; revise if misread. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Why test your poster on viewers?
questions.a: To check that the message is communicated clearly.

weeks.assessment_key: Poster rubric: 4 = message understood by both viewers, strong focal point, limited palette, readable lettering; 3 = minor issues; 2 = message unclear; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Bookmark musictheory.net (note duration, rest duration, time signatures). Get a bucket and drumsticks or wooden spoons, and a metronome app. Note values in 4/4: whole = 4 beats, half = 2, quarter = 1, eighth = ½, sixteenth = ¼.
misconceptions: Confusing beat and rhythm. Beat is the steady pulse; rhythm is the pattern of durations.
Rushing sixteenth notes. Count '1-e-and-a' evenly.

days.guide: Tap the steady beat, then the rhythm of three songs; explain the difference. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: What is the difference between beat and rhythm?
questions.a: The beat is the steady pulse; rhythm is the pattern of long and short sounds.

days.guide: Complete note and rest lessons; clap 8 patterns. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: How many sixteenth notes equal one quarter note?
questions.a: Four.

days.guide: Identify 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 by counting and conducting. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.a: Three beats per measure; the quarter note gets one beat.

days.guide: Play a 4-measure bucket rhythm with sixteenths from notation. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: How do you count four sixteenth notes?
questions.a: '1-e-and-a.'

days.guide: Rhythm reading test of 4 patterns with a metronome. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.q: How many beats does a dotted half note get in 4/4?
questions.a: Three.

weeks.assessment_key: Rhythm reading: 4 patterns at a steady metronome tempo (4 = all accurate; 3 = 3; 2 = 2; 1 = 0–1).

weeks.prep: Recorder (or keyboard/ukulele) and note-naming flashcards. Treble lines E G B D F, spaces F A C E; bass lines G B D F A ('Good Boys Do Fine Always'), spaces A C E G ('All Cows Eat Grass').
misconceptions: Using treble-clef names on bass clef. Each clef has its own line and space names.
Counting ledger lines incorrectly. Each ledger line continues the line-space pattern.

days.guide: Learn treble line and space notes; do a note-naming drill. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.a: F, A, C, E.

days.guide: Play B, A, G (recorder) or C-D-E (keyboard) and 'Hot Cross Buns.' Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: On recorder, which note uses only the thumb and first finger?
questions.a: B.

days.guide: Learn bass clef notes; name 20 in a timed drill. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Name the bass clef lines from bottom to top.
questions.a: G, B, D, F, A.

days.guide: Add two notes; play 'Mary Had a Little Lamb' and 'Ode to Joy' (first phrase). Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.a: A short line added above or below the staff for notes outside it.

days.guide: Note-naming quiz; play a short melody. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.q: What note is on the middle line of the treble staff?
questions.a: B.

weeks.assessment_key: Note-naming quiz: 20 notes in treble and bass (proficient 90%). Playing check: correct notes and steady beat in a short melody.

weeks.prep: Instrument, Chrome Music Lab (Piano Roll/Song Maker can switch to minor), and 'Ode to Joy' sheet music. Major scale pattern: W W H W W W H.
misconceptions: Thinking a half step skips a key. A half step is the very next key (white or black).
Practicing a whole piece at full speed with mistakes. Isolate trouble spots and slow down.

days.guide: Find whole and half steps on a keyboard; build C major. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Where are the half steps in C major?
questions.a: Between E–F and B–C.

days.guide: Listen to major and minor versions of a tune; describe moods. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: What changes when a major tune becomes minor?
questions.a: The third (and often sixth and seventh) notes are lowered, giving a darker sound.

days.guide: Practice 'Ode to Joy' using criteria; mark trouble spots. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.a: Steady tempo, correct notes, good tone.

days.guide: Slow-practice trouble spots with a metronome, gradually increasing. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.a: Accuracy first, then speed, so mistakes aren't practiced.

days.guide: Record the scale and melody; evaluate with criteria. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.a: A series of notes in order going up or down.

weeks.assessment_key: Recorded scale and melody: 4 = correct notes, steady tempo, good tone; 3 = minor errors; 2 = several; 1 = incomplete. Evaluation matches recording.

weeks.prep: Find Ravel's 'Bolero' and five excerpts at different tempos. Terms: pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff; crescendo; largo, adagio, andante, moderato, allegro, presto; legato (smooth), staccato (short).
misconceptions: Thinking 'piano' means the instrument. In dynamics, piano means soft.
Thinking a crescendo means faster. Crescendo means gradually louder.

days.guide: Listen to 'Bolero' and chart its dynamics; learn p, mp, mf, f. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: What happens to dynamics in Ravel's 'Bolero'?
questions.a: It grows in one long crescendo from very soft to very loud while the tempo stays steady.

days.guide: Learn tempo terms; match to five excerpts. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Put in order slow to fast: allegro, adagio, presto, andante.
questions.a: Adagio, andante, allegro, presto.

days.guide: Play a melody legato and staccato. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.a: Short, detached notes.

days.guide: Add dynamics and articulation to your melody and practice. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.a: Mezzo forte — medium loud.

days.guide: Terms quiz; perform with expression. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.a: Smooth and connected.

weeks.assessment_key: Terms quiz: dynamics (pp–ff), crescendo/decrescendo, tempo terms in order, legato/staccato. Proficient = 80%. Performance: follows marked dynamics and articulation.

weeks.prep: Print lyrics for 'Row, Row, Row Your Boat' and 'Dona Nobis Pacem' ('Grant us peace,' a traditional round in three parts). Find a recording of 'Dona Nobis Pacem.' Plan a mid-year family concert.
misconceptions: Singing from the throat. Use breath support from the diaphragm and good posture.
Listening to the other part and losing your own. Focus on your part; cover one ear if needed.

days.guide: Learn breathing and vocal warm-ups; sing do-re-mi-fa-sol-la-ti-do. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Name the solfege syllables of a major scale.
questions.a: Do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ti, do.

days.guide: Sing 'Row, Row, Row Your Boat' as a round. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.a: A song where voices sing the same melody starting at different times, creating harmony.

days.guide: Learn 'Dona Nobis Pacem'; sing one part with another. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.a: 'Grant us peace' (Latin).

days.guide: Rehearse a song and instrumental piece with performance criteria. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.a: Stand tall, shoulders relaxed, feet apart, chin level.

days.guide: Mid-year concert; self-evaluate. Set up a simple 'stage' and audience, have your child introduce the work, and hold applause until the end; afterward ask them to name one strength and one thing to improve before you add one specific comment.

questions.a: Two or more different pitches sounding at the same time.

weeks.assessment_key: Concert rubric (1–4 each): accurate pitch/notes, steady rhythm, tone and breath support, holds own part in a round, stage presence. Proficient = 3+ each.

weeks.prep: Find recordings: a sitar raga (e.g., Ravi Shankar), guzheng music, West African drumming (e.g., djembe ensemble), and mariachi ('El Son de la Negra'). Gather household percussion and a keyboard or xylophone app.
misconceptions: Thinking all world music uses Western scales and meters. Ragas, talas and pentatonic systems are different, complete musical systems.
Thinking polyrhythm is just playing fast. It's two or more different rhythms played at the same time.

days.guide: Listen to a raga; identify the drone (tanpura) and the tala cycle on tabla. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.a: A melodic framework in Indian classical music with specific notes, patterns and mood.

days.guide: Listen to guzheng; play a pentatonic melody on the black keys. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.a: A five-note scale (the black keys on a piano form one).

days.guide: Learn a 3-against-2 polyrhythm with two household instruments (one hits 3 evenly while the other hits 2 in the same time).

questions.a: Two or more contrasting rhythms played at the same time.

days.guide: Listen to mariachi; identify violins, trumpets, vihuela, guitarrón and the son jalisciense rhythm (alternating 6/8 and 3/4).

questions.q: Which mariachi instrument plays the bass?
questions.a: The guitarrón.

days.guide: Listening quiz identifying four traditions. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.a: A repeating rhythmic cycle in Indian music.

weeks.assessment_key: Listening quiz key: India — sitar, tabla, drone, raga/tala; China — guzheng, pentatonic; West Africa — djembe, polyrhythm, call and response; Mexico — mariachi, guitarrón, vihuela, trumpets, son rhythm. Proficient = 4/4 traditions identified with one feature each.

weeks.prep: Find recordings of Mozart's 'Twelve Variations on Ah vous dirai-je, Maman' (K. 265) and Beethoven's 'Für Elise.' Cut colored shapes for sections.
misconceptions: Thinking every return of A must be identical. Returning sections may vary slightly.
Confusing theme and variations with rondo. Variations change one theme repeatedly; rondo alternates a returning A with new sections.

days.guide: Label AB and ABA sections in songs. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.a: ABA — A, contrasting B, A returns.

days.guide: Map Für Elise as ABACA. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Which section of 'Für Elise' keeps returning?
questions.a: The famous opening A theme.

days.guide: Listen to Mozart's variations; describe three. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Name two ways Mozart varies the 'Twinkle' theme.
questions.a: Adding fast running notes, changing to minor, changing rhythm, moving the melody to the left hand.

days.guide: Compare form, purpose and mood of two pieces you like. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Why does form matter in music?
questions.a: It organizes the music, creating repetition and contrast so listeners can follow it.

days.guide: Listening quiz on forms. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.a: AB — two contrasting sections.

weeks.assessment_key: Form quiz: identifies AB, ABA, rondo and theme and variations in examples. Proficient = 80%. Written comparison addresses form, purpose and mood with specific details.

weeks.prep: Open Chrome Music Lab Song Maker; have staff paper and an instrument. Criteria: clear motif, A expresses a mood, B contrasts, A returns, ends with a cadence on the tonic.
misconceptions: Making A and B too similar. Change rhythm, register (high/low) or dynamics for contrast.
Ending on a note that sounds unfinished. End on the tonic (home note) for a final cadence.

days.guide: Improvise and record five short motifs. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.a: A short musical idea that can be repeated and developed.

days.guide: Compose an 8-measure A section expressing a mood. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: How can you make music sound happy?
questions.a: Major key, faster tempo, bright high notes.

days.guide: Compose a contrasting B section. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Name two ways to contrast B with A.
questions.a: Change register, rhythm, dynamics, tempo or major/minor.

days.guide: Notate or save the composition. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.a: So it can be performed again accurately.

days.guide: Play for a listener; record feedback using criteria. Treat it like a real event: quiet audience, a short spoken introduction and a bow; then debrief together using the week's rubric, starting with what went well.

questions.a: A musical ending of a phrase, like punctuation.

weeks.assessment_key: Draft: 4 = clear motif, 8-measure A, contrasting B, A returns, notated/saved, feedback recorded; 3 = one missing; 2 = two missing; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Find a public-domain Charlie Chaplin short (e.g., 'The Immigrant,' 1917) and an example of a famous leitmotif (e.g., the two-note 'Jaws' theme or Darth Vader's 'Imperial March').
misconceptions: Thinking film music should be noticed all the time. Often it supports the scene quietly.
Choosing music that doesn't match the action. Tempo and dynamics should follow events.

days.guide: Watch a scene with and without sound; describe how music changes meaning. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: How can music change the meaning of a scene?
questions.a: It sets mood and tells viewers how to feel—the same scene can seem scary or funny.

days.guide: Identify leitmotifs; create one for a character. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.a: A short musical theme associated with a character, place or idea.

days.guide: Create music or sound effects for a silent film clip. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.a: Matching hits and changes to on-screen events makes the scene more powerful.

days.guide: Revise the ABA composition; perform or play back. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.a: Answer varies; should cite feedback.

days.guide: Evaluate composition and film score; write a reflection. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: How did tempo or dynamics support your film scene?
questions.a: Answer varies; should link specific choices to action/mood.

weeks.assessment_key: Presentation: final ABA composition with revisions explained; film score synced to clip with a leitmotif. Rubric 1–4 for composition quality, sync and mood, reflection.

weeks.prep: Clear an open space; gather a few props (scarf, chair, hat). Recruit family members. Learn 'Yes, and' (accept an idea and add to it) and 'Freeze' (call freeze, tap someone out, start a new scene from the frozen pose).
misconceptions: Saying 'no' to scene partners' ideas. Accept ('yes') and build ('and') to keep scenes going.
Thinking tableaux are silly poses. Tableaux are frozen pictures that tell a story through levels, facial expression and focus.

days.guide: Do vocal and physical warm-ups; learn etiquette (listen, support others, no put-downs). Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.a: To prepare voice and body and focus the group.

days.guide: Play 'Yes, and' storytelling and 'Freeze' improv. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.a: Accept your partner's idea and add something new to it.

days.guide: Improvise scenes where characters want different things; name objectives. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.a: What the character wants in the scene.

days.guide: Create tableaux of three moments from a myth. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.a: Clear story, different levels, facial expressions and everyone focused on the action.

days.guide: Write about what made a scene work and what to change. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Why does conflict make scenes interesting?
questions.a: When characters want different things, there is tension and something at stake.

weeks.assessment_key: Participation rubric (1–4): commits to scenes, accepts and builds ideas, clear objectives, supports others. Reflection proficient if it names a specific successful moment and why.

weeks.prep: Find short monologues suitable for middle schoolers (e.g., from Aesop adaptations). Prepare a character profile template.
misconceptions: Speaking quietly on stage. Projection uses breath support, not shouting.
Moving randomly. Blocking and gestures should have purpose.

days.guide: Read one line in 6 emotions, changing pitch, pace and volume. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.a: The rise and fall of pitch in the voice.

days.guide: Walk as different characters leading with different body parts. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.a: Upright, chest leading, slow and confident.

days.guide: Choose a monologue; write a character profile. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.a: To understand the character's wants, fears and background so choices are believable.

days.guide: Memorize and rehearse with blocking. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.a: Planned movement and positions on stage.

days.guide: Perform and record reactions. Set up a simple 'stage' and audience, have your child introduce the work, and hold applause until the end; afterward ask them to name one strength and one thing to improve before you add one specific comment.

questions.a: Speaking loudly and clearly enough for the whole audience to hear.

weeks.assessment_key: Monologue rubric (1–4 each): memorized, projection and articulation, vocal variety, purposeful movement, character believability. Proficient = 3+ each.

weeks.prep: Choose an Aesop fable or Greek myth (e.g., 'The Tortoise and the Hare' or Perseus/Pegasus). Have a notebook; look at a sample script page showing character names, dialogue and stage directions in italics/parentheses.
misconceptions: Including every detail from the story. A script keeps only essential events and shows them through dialogue and action.
Writing narration instead of dialogue. Plays show story through what characters say and do.

days.guide: Identify the essential events (beginning, conflict, climax, resolution). Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: What is the climax of 'The Tortoise and the Hare'?
questions.a: The moment the tortoise passes the sleeping hare and crosses the finish line.

days.guide: Write a 2–3 page script with dialogue and stage directions. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.a: Instructions in a script for actors' movements, actions, and setting, often in italics or parentheses.

days.guide: Solve staging challenges with props, sound or movement. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: How could you show a storm on stage simply?
questions.a: Shake a sheet of cardboard for thunder, flicker lights, actors sway and use sound effects.

days.guide: Table read with family; revise. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.a: Actors read the script aloud together, seated, to hear how it works.

days.guide: Finalize script; plan props and costumes. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.a: A new version of a story changed to fit a different form, like a play.

weeks.assessment_key: Script rubric: 4 = essential events with clear conflict and resolution, formatted dialogue and stage directions, creative staging solutions; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = missing elements; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Script, simple costumes and props, a video camera. Mark stage areas with tape (upstage = away from audience, downstage = toward audience).
misconceptions: Turning your back to the audience. 'Cheat out' so the audience sees your face.
Stopping when you forget a line. Stay in character and improvise or let a partner help.

days.guide: Block entrances, exits and positions. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.a: The part of the stage closest to the audience.

days.guide: Rehearse with scripts, then off book for the first half. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.a: Performing without the script, from memory.

days.guide: Dress rehearsal with costumes and props. Set up a simple 'stage' and audience, have your child introduce the work, and hold applause until the end; afterward ask them to name one strength and one thing to improve before you add one specific comment.

questions.a: To practice everything exactly like the performance and fix problems.

days.guide: Perform for an audience and record it. Treat it like a real event: quiet audience, a short spoken introduction and a bow; then debrief together using the week's rubric, starting with what went well.

questions.a: A signal (a line, action or sound) for an actor or crew to do something.

days.guide: Watch the recording; write a critique using theatre vocabulary. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Name two theatre terms to use in a critique.
questions.a: Blocking, projection, objective, character, cue, tableau.

weeks.assessment_key: Performance: memorized, projected, in character, follows blocking. Critique rubric: 4 = evaluates specific choices with theatre terms and evidence; 3 = some terms; 2 = vague; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Phone or tablet camera; turn on the grid overlay. Find example photos showing rule of thirds, leading lines and framing.
misconceptions: Always centering the subject. Placing it on a rule-of-thirds intersection is often more interesting.
Taking every photo from standing eye level. Changing angle changes the mood and story.

days.guide: Study examples of rule of thirds, leading lines and framing. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: What is the rule of thirds?
questions.a: Dividing the frame into a 3×3 grid and placing important subjects along the lines or intersections.

days.guide: Take 10 photos using the grid; choose the best two. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Why is an off-center subject often more interesting?
questions.a: It creates balance with space and leads the eye through the image.

days.guide: Photograph an object from bird's-eye, eye-level and worm's-eye views. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: How does a worm's-eye view change a subject?
questions.a: It makes the subject look tall, powerful or dramatic.

days.guide: Neighborhood photo walk: leading lines, patterns, textures. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.a: Lines (roads, fences, rails) that draw the viewer's eye toward the subject.

days.guide: Select 5 best photos; caption the technique in each. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.a: Using objects in the scene (doorway, branches) to surround the subject.

weeks.assessment_key: 5-photo set: each uses an identified technique correctly with a caption explaining it. 4 = all 5; 3 = 4; 2 = 2–3; 1 = 0–1.

weeks.prep: Camera and a free photo editor (e.g., Snapseed, phone editing tools). Find a photo essay (e.g., a museum or news photo story).
misconceptions: Thinking photo edits are never misleading. Removing or adding objects can change the truth.
Shooting without a plan. A storyboard ensures a clear beginning, middle and end.

days.guide: Analyze a photo essay; identify beginning, middle and end. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What makes a photo essay tell a story?
questions.a: A sequence of images with a clear beginning, middle and end.

days.guide: Storyboard a 6-photo story about a routine or recipe. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.a: A sequence of sketches planning each shot.

days.guide: Take the photos following the storyboard. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.a: To show details and context and keep the story interesting.

days.guide: Crop and adjust contrast; discuss manipulation. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: When does editing become misleading manipulation?
questions.a: When it changes what actually happened—adding, removing or altering content to deceive.

days.guide: Present the photo story; gather feedback. Set up a simple 'stage' and audience, have your child introduce the work, and hold applause until the end; afterward ask them to name one strength and one thing to improve before you add one specific comment.

questions.a: The intensity of colors.

weeks.assessment_key: Photo story rubric: 4 = 6 photos follow storyboard with clear beginning/middle/end, varied shots, honest edits; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = unclear story; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Sticky notes (a pad), clay or LEGO figures, a free stop-motion app (e.g., Stop Motion Studio), and videos of a zoetrope and Muybridge's 'The Horse in Motion' (1878, filmed in Palo Alto, California).
misconceptions: Moving figures too much between frames. Small increments make smooth motion.
Thinking animation is one drawing that moves. It's many still images shown quickly.

days.guide: Make a 20-page flip book of a bouncing ball (squash on landing, stretch while falling). Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Why does a flip book appear to move?
questions.a: Images shown in quick succession blend together in our perception.

days.guide: Watch early animation; explain persistence of vision. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What did Muybridge's horse photos prove?
questions.a: That all four of a galloping horse's hooves leave the ground at the same time.

days.guide: Develop a 20–30 second idea with character, problem, solution. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: At 12 frames per second, how many photos for 20 seconds?
questions.a: 240 frames.

days.guide: Draw an 8-panel storyboard with camera angles. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.a: To show action clearly and add variety.

days.guide: Build characters and set. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Why should a set be stable?
questions.a: Bumping it between frames causes jumps in the animation.

weeks.assessment_key: Flip book: 20 pages with smooth bounce. Storyboard: 8 panels with character, problem, solution and camera angles. Proficient = both complete.

weeks.prep: Phone on a stand (or taped to a stack of books), stop-motion app, the set and characters. Use steady lamp light (not window light, which changes).
misconceptions: Changing lighting between frames, causing flicker. Use constant lamp light and close curtains.
Bumping the camera. Use a stand and a remote or timer.

days.guide: Shoot a 2-second test; adjust lighting and stability. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.a: To fix lighting, focus and stability before the full shoot.

days.guide: Shoot part 1, moving figures in small increments. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.a: Starting and stopping movements gradually with smaller moves for natural motion.

days.guide: Shoot part 2. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.a: Changing light between frames.

days.guide: Edit timing; add titles, credits and sound. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.a: To recognize everyone who helped and the music used.

days.guide: Screen for family; reflect. Set up a simple 'stage' and audience, have your child introduce the work, and hold applause until the end; afterward ask them to name one strength and one thing to improve before you add one specific comment.

questions.q: What would you improve next time?
questions.a: Answer varies; should be specific (e.g., smaller moves).

weeks.assessment_key: Animation rubric (1–4 each): smooth motion, clear story, stable camera/lighting, sound and credits. Proficient = 3+ each.

weeks.prep: Clear an open space; find video tutorials for Kalamatianos (Greek line dance in 7/8, counted slow-quick-quick), ballet folklórico zapateado, and a Bharatanatyam excerpt with mudras.
misconceptions: Thinking folk dances are just steps. They express community history, celebrations and identity.
Stomping hard for zapateado. Zapateado is controlled, rhythmic footwork with heel and toe strikes.

days.guide: Explore levels (low, middle, high), pathways (straight, curved, zigzag) and energy (sharp, smooth) moving across the room 10 ways.

questions.q: Name the three levels in dance.
questions.a: Low, middle and high.

days.guide: Learn basic Kalamatianos steps from a video. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What meter is the Kalamatianos danced in?
questions.a: 7/8 (slow-quick-quick).

days.guide: Learn the basic zapateado; discuss regional origin. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.a: Mexican folk dance that shows the regional dances and costumes of Mexico.

days.guide: Watch Bharatanatyam; try three mudras. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.a: Hand gestures that communicate meaning or tell a story.

days.guide: Write how one dance communicates its community's history or purpose. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.a: Tamil Nadu in South India.

weeks.assessment_key: Participation: tries all dances with effort and attention to steps. Written interpretation rubric: 4 = explains purpose and history of a dance with specific details; 3 = general explanation; 2 = vague; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Music without lyrics, a poem or natural phenomenon (water cycle, storm) as stimulus, and a recording device.
misconceptions: Making a dance of random moves. Strong choreography develops a few motifs.
Thinking canon and unison are the same. Unison = together; canon = staggered starts.

days.guide: Choose a stimulus; brainstorm movements. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What is a stimulus in choreography?
questions.a: The idea or source that inspires the dance.

days.guide: Create three motifs; vary level and speed. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.a: A short movement phrase that is repeated and varied.

days.guide: Arrange motifs into a 1-minute dance with beginning, middle and end. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: Why have a clear beginning and ending?
questions.a: So the audience knows when the dance starts and ends and can follow its shape.

days.guide: Rehearse with a partner using unison and canon. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.a: Dancers perform the same movement starting at different times.

days.guide: Perform, record and explain the connection to the stimulus. Set up a simple 'stage' and audience, have your child introduce the work, and hold applause until the end; afterward ask them to name one strength and one thing to improve before you add one specific comment.

questions.q: How does your dance connect to the stimulus?
questions.a: Answer varies; should link specific motifs to parts of the stimulus.

weeks.assessment_key: Choreography rubric (1–4 each): three motifs developed, clear structure, unison and canon, connection to stimulus explained. Proficient = 3+ each.

weeks.prep: Review the sketchbook 'ideas' page; gather the child's chosen media.
misconceptions: Picking a theme that's too broad. Narrow it to a specific idea you can show.
Waiting until the end for feedback. Mid-process feedback helps.

days.guide: Review ideas; choose a personally meaningful theme. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.a: It connects to your experiences, interests or values.

days.guide: Make three thumbnails; choose media. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.a: Different media create different effects suited to the idea.

days.guide: Begin the culminating artwork. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: What is a concept in art?
questions.a: The idea or message behind an artwork.

days.guide: Continue; get mid-point feedback. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.a: 'What do you think this artwork is about?' — to check the message.

days.guide: Complete and reflect on whether it conveys intended meaning. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: How do you know if your art conveys meaning?
questions.a: Viewers can describe the intended idea; elements and principles support it.

weeks.assessment_key: Culminating artwork rubric (1–4 each): clear personal concept, purposeful media and techniques, use of elements/principles, craftsmanship, reflection. Proficient = 3+ each.

weeks.prep: Plan a local or virtual museum visit (Getty or LACMA online). Get graph paper for the display plan.
misconceptions: Thinking museums show everything they own. Curators select and arrange works to tell stories.
Thinking display order doesn't matter. Flow guides how viewers experience the show.

days.guide: Visit a museum; note how works are grouped and labeled. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Name two ways museums group artworks.
questions.a: By time period, culture, artist, theme or medium.

days.guide: Write how the museum's choices reflect community values. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: How can a museum reflect its community?
questions.a: By collecting and showing art from local cultures and histories.

days.guide: Select 8–10 works across visual and media arts. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.a: Growth, variety, best quality and a theme.

days.guide: Draw a display plan with placement and flow. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.a: To lead viewers through the exhibition in a meaningful order.

days.guide: Share the plan; revise based on feedback. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.a: A small sign with title, artist, media, date and a short description.

weeks.assessment_key: Museum reflection: 4 = describes grouping/labels and connects choices to community values with examples; 3 = some; 2 = vague; 1 = missing. Display plan: 8–10 works placed with clear flow.

weeks.prep: Selected artworks, construction paper for mats, labels, and a camera for the digital portfolio.
misconceptions: Writing an artist statement that only lists projects. It should explain growth, interests and ideas.
Leaving out media arts and music. A complete portfolio includes animation and recordings.

days.guide: Write a one-paragraph artist statement. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: What belongs in an artist statement?
questions.a: Your interests, ideas, techniques you used and how you grew.

days.guide: Write wall labels for each piece. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.a: 'City Corner, colored pencil, 2027. Two-point perspective shows a busy street.'

days.guide: Mat and mount 2D works; prepare stands for 3D. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.a: It frames and protects the work and looks professional.

days.guide: Photograph works and assemble a digital portfolio with animation and music. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.a: It preserves work and is easy to share.

days.guide: Evaluate completeness with a checklist. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.a: Artworks, labels, artist statement, digital portfolio, recordings.

weeks.assessment_key: Portfolio checklist: 8–10 works, labels, matting, digital portfolio including animation and music. Artist statement rubric: 4 = growth, interests and specific techniques; 3 = most; 2 = list only; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Exhibition space, instrument, audience invitations, and comment cards for visitors.
misconceptions: Thinking a docent only reads labels. A docent explains, answers questions and engages visitors.
Ignoring visitor feedback. Comments help you grow.

days.guide: Install the exhibition following the plan. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.a: Center at about eye level (around 57–60 inches).

days.guide: Rehearse a music piece and a dance or monologue. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: What should you rehearse besides the piece itself?
questions.a: Introductions, transitions and bows.

days.guide: Host the showcase as docent; perform. Set up a simple 'stage' and audience, have your child introduce the work, and hold applause until the end; afterward ask them to name one strength and one thing to improve before you add one specific comment.

questions.a: A guide who leads visitors and explains artworks.

days.guide: Collect and summarize visitor comments. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: What patterns did you notice in comments?
questions.a: Answer varies; should summarize common themes.

days.guide: Write a final reflection; set a grade 7 arts goal. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What was your favorite project and why?
questions.a: Answer varies; should name the project and a specific reason.

weeks.assessment_key: Showcase rubric (1–4 each): installation quality, docent talk, performance, response to feedback. Reflection proficient if it names a favorite project with reasons, growth evidence, and a specific grade 7 goal.
